summary: This unit teaches you to cut steel bar, sections, tube and sheet safely and accurately with hand tools and cutting machines: hacksaws, snips, tube cutters, guillotines, bandsaws, cold saws and abrasive cut-off saws. You will learn to plan cuts from a cutting list with little waste, mark out, choose and set up the right tool, keep guards and isolation in place, check and deburr the parts, and clean up and report faults.

blocks.p: **Mechanical cutting** means cutting metal by sawing, shearing or grinding, rather than by melting or burning it with a flame or an arc. Nearly every fabrication job starts with it: bars and tubes cut to length for frames, gates and shelving; angle mitred for corners; sheet sheared and snipped into blanks for trays, guards and ducts.

Accurate cutting makes everything that follows easier. Parts cut to length and square fit up quickly and weld straight; parts cut badly have to be trimmed, packed or scrapped. Cutting machines are also among the most dangerous in the workshop, so this unit is as much about safe working as about method.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who cuts metal in a fabrication shop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely
Use guards, PPE and isolation; know the emergency stop; handle bar and sheet safely.
Plan the cuts
Read the drawing and cutting list, check the stock, plan the cuts to keep waste low, and allow for the saw cut.
Mark out
Mark lengths, squares and mitres accurately from a datum, with the waste side marked.
Cut with hand tools
Choose, fit and use hacksaw blades; use snips, tube cutters, bolt cutters and chisels correctly.
Cut with machines
Set up and use guillotines, bandsaws, power hacksaws, cold saws and abrasive cut-off saws safely.
Check and finish
Deburr parts, check size, squareness and mitres against the tolerance, and deal with parts that are out.
Clean up and report
Isolate machines, clear chips safely, sort offcuts, look after tools, and report and tag out faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safety, guarding, isolation, planning, hand sawing, snips, shearing, power saws, abrasive cutting, checking and clean-up.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as TPI, kerf, swarf, tension, bi-metal) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: cutting angle and square tube to a cutting list, with some 45° mitres, by hand and on a power saw; and cutting sheet blanks for small trays on a guillotine, with notches and a curve cut by snips. The assessor watches your safety, set-up and checking as well as the finished parts.

blocks.note: When you practise, check every part you cut before you cut the next one. The habit of checking as you go is what the assessor most wants to see, and it is what saves material in a real shop.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Cuts and amputation
Blades and guillotines cut fingers off; sheet edges and offcuts are razor sharp
Guards in place and set close to the work
Hands well clear of blades; never reach across a moving blade
Gloves for handling sheet and offcuts
Entanglement
Turning blades, drills and spindles catch loose clothing, gloves, hair, rings and chains and pull you in
Close-fitting overalls, sleeves buttoned
Hair tied back; rings, watches and chains off
No loose gloves near a turning blade or drill
Flying particles
Chips, sparks and pieces of a broken blade or disc fly out at speed
Safety glasses always; a face shield for abrasive saws and grinders
Stand to one side of a disc's line
Crushing
A guillotine's hold-down can crush fingers; heavy bars and sheets fall
Fingers kept behind the guard
Safety boots; work held firmly
Noise
Saws, abrasive discs and shears damage hearing over time
Ear plugs or muffs at power saws and abrasive cutters
Fire and burns
Abrasive cutting throws hot sparks; cut ends get hot
Sparks pointed away from people and anything that can burn
Treat cut ends as hot
Electricity
Damaged leads and plugs on portable tools give shocks
Check leads and plugs before use; report damage
Manual handling
Long bars and big sheets strain backs and swing into people
Lift correctly; two people for long bars and large sheets

ul: Guards keep your hands away from the blade and catch flying pieces. They must **always be in place**, set as close to the work as the machine allows (on a bandsaw, the blade guides and guard are brought down close to the work, so little blade is left bare).
Never remove, wedge open or work round a guard to make a job quicker.
If a guard is **missing or damaged**, do not use the machine. Switch it off, tag it DO NOT USE and tell your instructor.

head: PPE
When
rows: Safety glasses with side shields
At all times in the workshop
Face shield over safety glasses
Abrasive cut-off saws and angle grinders
Ear plugs or muffs
Power saws, abrasive cutting and noisy shears
Safety boots
At all times: bars and sheets are heavy and sharp
Leather or cut-resistant gloves
Handling sheet, bar and offcuts, and at the abrasive saw, but **not** near the blade of a bandsaw, a drill or other turning parts that can catch a loose glove
Close-fitting overalls
At all times; no loose sleeves, ties or scarves

blocks.p: The **emergency stop** is a large red mushroom-shaped button, often on a yellow background. It stops the machine at once. Find it **before** you start any machine. After it has been used, the machine is checked before it is restarted. A machine whose emergency stop does not work must not be used.
Before you change a blade, clear a jam, adjust a guide inside a guard or clean round the blade, **isolate** the machine so nobody can start it while your hands are inside.

flow: Switch off at the machine and wait for the blade or disc to stop completely
Switch off at the isolator, or unplug a plug-in tool
Fit your own padlock to the isolator, with a tag giving your name, the date and the reason
Try the start button to prove the machine will not start, then return it to off
Do the work, with gloves and the right tools
Refit every guard, then remove your lock and tag and test the machine

blocks.note: A machine that is only switched off at its own switch can be switched on by someone who does not know you are working on it. Only your own lock on the isolator keeps you safe.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Carry long bars with **two people**, one at each end, holding them level. Warn people at doors and corners.
Carry sheet on its edge, with gloves; two people for large sheets. Never slide your hand along a sheet edge.
Store bar on racks and sheet in sheet racks, never leaning loose against walls or benches where it can slide and fall.

blocks.note: Many small shops work with their doors open to the street. Keep passers-by and customers out of the line of sparks and away from the machines, and never let a long bar swing out of the door into the road.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Planning the cuts and marking out

ul: Read the drawing and the **cutting list**: each part's mark, length, number needed, section (for example 25 × 25 × 3 angle or 25 mm square tube) and how its ends are cut (square or mitred).
Check the stock: the right section and thickness, straight, and free of deep rust and damage. Bar, angle and tube usually come in 6 m lengths; sheet often as 1 220 mm × 2 440 mm (4 ft × 8 ft).
Check the tolerance on the drawing, for example ±1 mm.
Cut the **longest pieces first**, then fit shorter pieces into what is left.
Allow for the **kerf**, the width of each saw cut: about 1 mm for a hacksaw and about 1–3 mm for power saws and abrasive discs, depending on the blade.
Allow a few millimetres to **square the first end**: stock ends are rarely square or clean.
Nest mitred pieces head to tail along the bar, so one cut makes two mitres.
Write the plan down, length by length, and tick the pieces off as they are cut.

head: One 6 m length of angle
Uses
rows: Square the first end
5 mm
2 pieces at 1 500 mm
3 pieces at 900 mm
5 saw cuts at about 2 mm each
10 mm
Offcut left

ul: Measure every piece from a **squared end** or another datum, not from the last mark, so small errors do not add up.
Use an engineer's square and a **scriber** for a fine, exact line on bright steel. Paint the area with **marking blue** first so the line shows clearly.
On rough hot-rolled steel, a fine soapstone line or a fine marker shows better.
On **galvanised or painted** sheet, use a fine marker or pencil for any line that stays on the finished part: a scribed line cuts through the coating and soon rusts.
Mark 45° mitres with the 45° face of a combination square. Check on the drawing whether the length is to the long point or the short point of the mitre.
Mark round tube with a wraparound strip so the line meets itself square.
Put a **cross on the waste side** of every line, so the cut is made on the right side.
When many pieces are the same length, set a **length stop** on the saw instead of marking each piece, and check the first piece (see Checking).

blocks.note: Cut on the waste side of the line, with the edge of the kerf just touching the line. The saw's width then comes out of the waste, and the part stays full size.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A hacksaw has a **frame**, a **handle**, a **blade** held on two pins, and a **wing nut** that sets the blade's **tension**. Most frames take 300 mm blades, and some adjust for 250 mm. A **junior hacksaw** with a small blade is used for light work.

head: TPI (teeth per inch, about 25 mm)
Use it for
rows: Large solid sections and soft metals, where coarse teeth clear the chips quickly
General solid bar and thick sections in mild steel
Angle, heavier tube and conduit, and metal about 3–6 mm thick
Thin-wall tube and thin sheet, under about 3 mm

blocks.p: **TPI** means teeth per inch (25.4 mm). The rule is that **at least three teeth** must touch the work at all times. With fewer, each tooth catches on the thin edge like a step, snags, and snaps off.

head: Blade type
Points to know
rows: Carbon steel
Cheap; hard blades break easily, flexible ones blunt quickly
High-speed steel (HSS)
Hard and long-lasting, but brittle: it snaps if twisted
Bi-metal
A hard high-speed steel toothed edge joined to a flexible back: long life and hard to break; the best choice for most workshop sawing

flow: Choose the TPI for the thinnest part of the section you are cutting
Fit the blade with the **teeth pointing forward**, away from the handle, because a hacksaw cuts on the push stroke
Tighten the wing nut until the blade is firm and does not flex sideways
Check that the blade is straight in the frame, not twisted
Clamp the work in the vice with the cut line **close to the jaws**, so it cannot vibrate (chatter)
Stand comfortably, one hand on the handle and one on the front of the frame
Start on the waste side of the line on a **flat face**, not on a sharp corner, guiding the blade with your thumb or a small file nick
Use slow, steady, **full-length strokes**, about one a second or a little slower; press on the forward stroke and ease off on the return
Keep the saw upright and the blade in line, and let the teeth do the work
Ease off as you finish, and support the offcut so it does not snap off and tear the edge

ul: Turn the work so the blade cuts across the widest section it can: saw angle across both legs, and turn a tube as you go, so you do not end up cutting a thin wall edge-on.
For a deep cut, turn the blade through 90° in the frame so the frame clears the work.
If a blade breaks part-way through, **start a new cut from another side**. A new blade is slightly wider than the worn one and will jam in the old cut.
A blade that wanders, breaks or loses teeth tells you something: see the faults table in Checking.

head: Snips
Use
Note
rows: Straight-cut snips (often yellow handles)
Straight lines and gentle curves
Open wide and make long cuts
Left-cut snips (often red handles)
Curves turning to the left
The waste curls away on the right
Right-cut snips (often green handles)
Curves turning to the right
The waste curls away on the left
Tinman's snips
Straight and curved cuts in thin sheet
Heavier blades; straight and curved patterns
Bench or lever shears
Thicker sheet and flat bar, within their marked capacity
Fixed to the bench; long lever

ul: Check that the sheet is within the snips' capacity, which the maker gives (often about 1.2 mm mild steel for aviation snips, and less for stainless steel).
For a straight cut, **do not close the tips fully** at the end of each cut. Closing the tips leaves a small step or tear in the edge; stop short and feed in again.
For a curve or a hole, cut away most of the waste first, then follow the line with short cuts, turning the sheet as you go.
Wear gloves and safety glasses: the edges and curls of waste are razor sharp. Put waste straight in the scrap bin.

head: Tool
Use
Good practice
rows: Wheel tube cutter
Cutting copper, aluminium and thin steel tube cleanly and square
Tighten the knob only a little (about a quarter turn) after each full turn round the tube, or the tube squashes; remove the inside burr with the reamer
Bolt cutters (croppers)
Cutting rod, bolts, wire and mesh
Stay within the marked capacity; never cut hardened steel unless the cutters are rated for it; no extension handles; hold the free end, as it flies
Cold chisel and hammer
Shearing sheet held in the vice, cutting off rivet and bolt heads
Grind a mushroomed head back to shape before use; cut away from people; wear safety glasses
Files
Removing burrs and dressing edges to the line
Always with a handle fitted; clean with a file card; stroke along the edge

blocks.p: A **guillotine** shears sheet in a straight line between a fixed bottom blade and a moving top blade. Workshop guillotines are worked by a **foot pedal** (treadle) or by a motor.

head: Part
Its job
rows: Top and bottom blades
Shear the sheet; the top blade is set at a slight angle (rake) so it cuts progressively across the sheet
Hold-down
Clamps the sheet firmly just before the blade cuts, so it cannot lift or move
Finger guard
Keeps fingers out of the hold-down and the blade
Back gauge (back stop)
Sets the width of the piece being cut
Side guide (squaring arm)
Holds the sheet square to the blade
Capacity plate
States the thickest mild steel and the longest cut the machine is built for

ul: The capacity plate gives the limit for **mild steel**. Stronger metals need more force, so a guillotine can cut much less thickness of **stainless steel**, often only about two-thirds as thick, and spring steel or hardened material not at all.
Never cut rod, bar, wire or anything thicker or harder than the plate allows: it damages the blades and can throw pieces out.
Never cut strips so narrow that the hold-down cannot grip them, or pieces so short that your fingers would have to go near the guard.

flow: Read the capacity plate and check that the guard and hold-down are in place and working
Put on safety glasses, boots and gloves for handling the sheet
Set the back gauge to the size needed, or mark the line on the sheet
Make sure nobody else is near the blade, the back of the machine or the pedal
Slide the sheet in from the front, square against the side guide, until it touches the back gauge (or the line sits on the blade's edge)
Keep both hands on the sheet in front of the guard, well clear of the hold-down and the blade
Press the pedal firmly in one smooth stroke
Remove the piece, check its size, and put offcuts straight in the scrap bin

blocks.note: Only **one person** works a guillotine: the person holding the sheet also works the pedal. A helper on the pedal cannot see where the operator's hands are.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check the **first piece** cut against the back gauge for size and squareness before cutting the rest.
A heavy burr, or a cut edge that is bent or torn, means blunt blades or the wrong blade clearance for the thickness. Stop and report it: setting the blades is a job for a trained person.

A **nibbler** (hand-held power tool) cuts sheet in many small bites, so it can follow curves and inside shapes and cause little distortion. Its small, crescent-shaped chips are sharp and spread far: sweep them up.
**Throatless shears** let the sheet move freely past the blades, so they can cut curves as well as straight lines.
A **universal steelworker (ironworker)** shears flat bar and angle, punches holes and cuts notches. One operator only, with the hold-down and guards set for each job.

blocks.p: A **horizontal bandsaw** cuts with a continuous blade running round two wheels. The saw arm lowers the blade through the work, and the vice holds the work square. It cuts bar, tube and sections quickly and accurately, with a narrow kerf, and a **length stop** lets you cut many pieces to the same length.

flow: Check the machine: guards fitted, blade sharp and correctly tensioned, the right blade for the job, coolant topped up, emergency stop working
Mark the length on the bar or set the length stop
Clamp the bar firmly in the vice, square to the blade; support a long bar on a roller stand at the same height
Bring the blade guides close to the work
Set the speed and the feed for the material and section: slower for hard metals and large sections
Turn on the coolant, start the machine and lower the blade gently onto the work
Keep hands clear while it cuts; never reach across the blade
Let the blade stop before you take the piece out; check it, deburr it, and clear chips with a brush

head: What the chips look like
What it means
rows: Thin, curled, silvery chips
Speed and feed about right
Blue or brown, burnt-looking chips
Too much speed or feed, or not enough coolant: the blade is overheating
Fine powder
Feed too light or the blade blunt: the teeth are rubbing, not cutting

ul: Bandsaw blades often have **variable pitch** teeth (for example 6/10 or 10/14 teeth per inch). The same three-teeth rule applies: finer teeth for thin-wall tube, coarser for large solid bar.
**Coolant** keeps the blade cool so it stays sharp and lasts longer, and washes the chips out of the cut.
If the blade breaks, hit the emergency stop or switch off, keep clear until everything has stopped, and report it. Never reach in to pull a broken blade out of a running machine.

blocks.h: The power hacksaw and the cold saw

ul: A **power hacksaw** moves a straight blade back and forth and lifts it on the return stroke. It is slower than a bandsaw but simple and reliable. Fit the blade as the machine's marking shows, clamp the work in its vice, and use coolant on steel.
A **cold saw** cuts with a toothed circular blade turning slowly, with coolant. It gives very square, clean cuts with little burr and cool ends, and its vice swivels for accurate mitres.

blocks.p: An **abrasive cut-off saw** ("chop saw") cuts with a thin, reinforced, resin-bonded disc spinning at high speed. It cuts steel quickly, including mitres, but a disc that breaks can throw pieces out with great force.

head: Check on the disc
Why
rows: Its maximum speed (rpm or m/s) is at least the saw's speed
A disc run faster than its rating can burst
It is the right size and type (for steel, or for stainless steel)
Wrong discs cut badly, overheat and may break
It is undamaged: no cracks, chips or bends, and it has not been dropped or got wet
Damage or damp weakens the bond
It is within its use-by date, if the centre ring shows one
The resin bond weakens with age
It is fitted with the right flanges, and the guard is in place and moves freely
A loose or badly fitted disc wobbles and breaks

flow: Check the disc and the guard; clear anything that can burn from the line of the sparks, and make sure nobody stands in that line
Put on safety glasses and a face shield, hearing protection and gloves
Clamp the work firmly in the saw's vice so it cannot move or twist
Stand to one side, out of line with the disc; start the saw and let it reach full speed (let a newly fitted disc run for a short time first, as the Centre's rule says)
Lower the disc with light, steady pressure and let it cut; never force it, twist it or push it sideways
Let the disc stop before you lift the work out; treat the cut ends as hot and sharp

ul: Never cut or grind with the **side** of a thin cutting disc: side loads can shatter it.
If the disc wobbles or vibrates, switch off, let it stop and check it before going on.
Pushing hard does not cut faster: it overheats the work (blue, burnt ends), glazes or wears the disc, and raises the risk of breakage.
Store discs flat, in a dry place, in their packaging.

blocks.h: The angle grinder with a cutting disc

ul: Use the guard, the side handle and **both hands**. Unplug the grinder before changing the disc.
The disc must be rated for at least the grinder's speed and be the right size for its guard: never fit a larger disc than the guard is made for.
Support the work so the cut opens as you go rather than closing and pinching the disc, which makes the grinder kick back.
Let the disc stop before you put the grinder down, and point the sparks away from people and anything that can burn.

blocks.p: A **hole saw** is a round, toothed cutter on a drill, with a pilot drill in its centre, for large round holes in sheet and thin plate. Clamp the work, run larger hole saws at a slow speed, use cutting fluid on steel, and hold the drill firmly with both hands: a hole saw that catches can twist the drill hard.

head: Job
Best choice
rows: Many bars or tubes cut to the same length, square
Bandsaw or cold saw with a length stop
A few cuts on bar, angle or tube
Hacksaw or abrasive cut-off saw
45° mitres on tube or angle
Cold saw or bandsaw with a swivel vice, or an abrasive saw
Straight cuts in sheet
Guillotine
Curves, notches and inside shapes in sheet
Snips or a nibbler
Copper or thin steel tube
Wheel tube cutter
Rod, bolts and mesh
Bolt cutters
Large round holes in sheet
Hole saw
Cutting on site, away from the bench saws
Hacksaw, or an angle grinder used with great care

blocks.p: A **burr** is the thin, sharp ridge of metal pushed up along a cut edge. Remove it from every part: it cuts hands, it makes measurements wrong, and it stops parts sitting flat and square for welding.

ul: File the burr off with a few light strokes along the edge, holding the file at a slight angle.
Use a deburring tool or a flap disc for long edges, and a reamer or round file inside tube.
**Length:** measure each part with a steel rule or tape from the squared end, and compare it with the cutting list and its tolerance.
**Squareness:** hold an engineer's square against the side and the cut end and look for light between them.
**Mitres:** check each with the 45° face of a combination square, and put two mitred ends together: they should make a true 90° corner.
**Edges:** straight and clean, without deep saw marks, tears or heat damage.
**Count and label** the pieces against the cutting list, so the right parts go to the welder.

blocks.note: When cutting many pieces against a length stop, cut **one**, measure it and adjust the stop, then cut the rest, measuring every few pieces. A stop can be set wrongly or creep, and every piece after it will be wrong.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Dealing with a part that is out

head: What you find
What to do
rows: Within tolerance and square
Deburr, label and stack it with the set
Too long
Trim it back and measure again
Out of square, but long enough to trim
Square the end again, then check the length
Too short, or out of square and too short to trim
Do not use it: mark it rejected, set it aside and tell the instructor, so a new piece is cut and the cause is found

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Hacksaw cut wanders off the line
Blade loose
Saw twisted or not upright
Teeth worn on one side
Tension the blade; keep the saw upright with steady strokes; fit a new blade
Hacksaw blade snaps
Too much pressure, or twisting
Blade loose, or work loose in the vice
Too few teeth in contact
Steady, even pressure; tension the blade; clamp the work; choose a finer blade
Teeth strip off
Blade too coarse for thin wall or sheet
Starting on a sharp corner
Finer blade; start on a flat face at a slight angle
Bandsaw cut not square
Blunt blade
Guides set too far apart or worn
Blade tension low; feed too heavy
New blade; guides close to the work; correct tension and feed
Blue chips; blade blunts quickly
Speed or feed too high; coolant low or off
Reduce speed or feed; check the coolant
Guillotine leaves a heavy burr, or bends the edge
Blades blunt
Blade clearance wrong for the thickness
Sheet too thick or too hard
Stop and report; keep within the capacity
Snipped edge stepped or torn
Tips closed fully at the end of each cut
Blunt snips; sheet too thick
Stop short of the tips; sharp snips within their capacity
Abrasive cut ends blue; disc wears fast or glazes
Too much pressure; wrong disc
Light, steady pressure; the right disc for the metal

sections.title: Clean-up, care of tools and reporting

blocks.h: At the end of the job

flow: Switch off and isolate the machines, and wait for blades and discs to stop
Clear chips and swarf with a **brush** or a hook, never with your hands and never by blowing them with an air line
Put swarf in the metal swarf bin; wipe up coolant and oil so nobody slips
Sort the offcuts: useful lengths labelled and back to the rack, the rest in the scrap bin; sharp pieces never left on the floor
Check blades and discs for wear and damage; release blade tension if the Centre's rule says so
Wipe the machines down and lightly oil bare steel surfaces where the maker says
Clean hand tools (snips, hacksaws, files, squares, tapes) and put them back in their places
Sweep the floor and leave the area safe for the next person

blocks.note: In Jamaica's humid air, bare steel on saw tables, vices and hand tools rusts quickly, and abrasive discs can take up damp. Oil bare surfaces lightly and keep discs dry in their packaging.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Damaged or missing guards
A cracked bandsaw guard, a missing guillotine finger guard
Do not use the machine; tag it DO NOT USE; report it
Faulty controls
An emergency stop that does nothing, a switch that sticks
Tag it out of use at once and report it: it must be repaired before anyone uses it
Blades and discs
A blunt, cracked or broken blade; a disc that wobbles or is damaged
Stop, isolate and report; replace only if you are trained and allowed to
Strange noise, smell or vibration
A grinding noise, a burning smell, a shaking saw
Switch off, isolate and report
Spills and hazards
Coolant leaking onto the floor
Clean it up, put out a warning if needed, and report the leak
Injuries and near misses
A cut, a chip in the eye, a disc that shattered
First aid, then report and record it so the cause is fixed
Stock
Blades, discs or material running low
Tell the instructor or storekeeper so more can be ordered

blocks.note: Reporting a fault is not getting someone into trouble. It is how the next person is kept safe, and it is part of the standard you are assessed against.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of cutting tools and machines and say how guards, PPE and safe habits control them.
I can find and use the emergency stop, and isolate and lock out a machine before working on it.
I can carry long bars and sheets safely.
I can read a cutting list, check the stock and plan the cuts to keep waste low, allowing for the kerf.
I can mark out lengths, squares and mitres accurately from a datum, with the waste side marked.
I can choose a hacksaw blade by its TPI, fit it with the teeth forward and the right tension, and saw straight.
I can choose and use snips for straight cuts and curves without stepping the edge.
I can use a tube cutter, bolt cutters, a cold chisel and files correctly.
I can check a guillotine's capacity and cut sheet on it safely, alone at the machine.
I can set up a bandsaw, read its chips, and cut bars to length against a stop.
I can check, fit and use an abrasive cut-off saw safely.
I can choose the right tool or machine for a cutting job.
I can deburr parts and check them for length, squareness and mitre angle.
I can decide what to do with a part that is too long, too short or out of square.
I can name common cutting faults, their causes and cures.
I can clean up safely, look after tools and machines, and report and tag out faults.

terms: Back gauge
The adjustable stop at the back of a guillotine that sets the width of a cut
Bi-metal blade
A blade with a hard toothed edge joined to a flexible back
Burr
A thin, sharp ridge of metal left on a cut edge
Capacity plate
The plate on a machine stating the largest size or thickness it is built to cut
Coolant
Liquid that cools the blade and clears chips from the cut
Cutting list
A list of the pieces to be cut, with their sizes, numbers and material
Datum
The end, edge or line that measurements are taken from
Emergency stop
A large red button that stops a machine at once
Guard
A cover that keeps hands away from a blade and catches flying pieces
Guillotine
A machine that shears sheet in a straight line between two blades
Hold-down
The clamp on a guillotine that holds the sheet still during the cut
Hole saw
A round toothed cutter on a drill for cutting large holes
Isolation
Cutting off and locking off the power so a machine cannot be started
Kerf
The width of the cut made by a blade or disc
Length stop
A stop on a saw that sets every piece to the same length
Lock-out
Fitting your own padlock and tag to an isolator while you work on a machine
Marking blue
Blue marking fluid that makes scribed lines show clearly on steel
Mitre
An end cut at an angle, usually 45°, so two parts make a corner
Nibbler
A tool that cuts sheet in many small bites
Snips
Hand shears for cutting sheet metal
Swarf
Small chips and waste left by sawing or drilling
Tension
The tightness of a blade in its frame or on its wheels
TPI
Teeth per inch: the number of teeth in each 25 mm of blade

c1.title: Steel shelving for a hardware store in Linstead
c1.text: Tamoy and two classmates are cutting parts for heavy steel shelving for a hardware store in Linstead, St Catherine. The cutting list calls for twelve uprights 1 950 mm long and twenty-four shelf rails 1 200 mm long, all in 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle, within ±1 mm. The angle comes in 6 m lengths. They are using a horizontal bandsaw with a length stop; its kerf is about 2 mm.

c2.title: A church railing in Highgate
c2.text: Fabian is repairing the railing on the steps of a church in Highgate, St Mary. He must cut out damaged lengths of 25 mm square tube with 1.5 mm walls, and some 12 mm solid round bar, on site with a hacksaw. The only blades in his toolbox are 18 TPI.

c3.title: Galvanised trays for a fish market in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Jodi-Ann is cutting 1.0 mm galvanised steel sheet into blanks for drainage trays for a fish market in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The workshop's foot-operated guillotine has a capacity plate that reads MILD STEEL 1.6 mm, 1 250 mm. Each blank also needs two corner notches and one rounded corner, which she cuts with snips.

c4.title: Burglar-bar frames in Ewarton
c4.text: Kadeem works in a small shop in Ewarton, St Catherine, cutting 40 mm square tube for burglar-bar frames on an abrasive cut-off saw. A box of new cutting discs got soaked in a storm last month and has since dried out. A freshly painted gate is drying on trestles about 3 m behind the saw, in the line of the sparks. The saw's tube clamp has been sticking.

c5.title: Closing down the bandsaw in Black River
c5.text: At the end of the day in a fabrication shop in Black River, St Elizabeth, Oshane is asked to clean the horizontal bandsaw. Chips and spilled coolant cover the floor round it. Earlier, a classmate found that the bandsaw's emergency stop did nothing when pressed, but carried on using the saw.

questions.q: Why can Tamoy not get five 1 200 mm rails from one 6 m length of angle?
o: The bandsaw's length stop cannot be set for lengths over 1 m
Five rails need 6 000 mm plus the saw cuts and squaring the end
Angle stretches slightly as it is cut, so each piece comes out long
Each rail must have 50 mm extra left on it for trimming later
questions.why: Five rails take exactly 6 000 mm before any cutting, and every cut removes about 2 mm, with a few millimetres more to square the first end. So only four full rails come from a length; the plan must allow for the kerf.

questions.q: Tamoy has set the length stop for the uprights. What should she do before cutting all twelve?
o: Cut all twelve, then measure them together at the end
Measure the stop's distance once with a tape, then cut them all
Cut one, measure it and adjust the stop, then check every few
Mark every piece by hand as well, in case the stop is wrong
questions.why: A first-off check proves the stop is set right before material is wasted, and checking every few pieces catches a stop that creeps. Measuring only at the end can leave twelve wrong uprights.

questions.q: Partway through the job, the chips coming off the bandsaw are blue and the blade is very hot. What should Tamoy do?
o: Reduce the speed or the feed and check the coolant
Increase the feed so the cut is finished sooner
Carry on: blue chips show the blade is cutting well
Switch the coolant off so it does not boil on the blade
questions.why: Blue, burnt chips mean the blade is overheating from too much speed or feed or too little coolant. Thin, curled, silvery chips are the sign of a blade cutting well.

questions.q: Each 6 m length sticks out more than 4 m beyond the saw's vice. How should it be held?
o: Have a classmate hold the far end up by hand during the cut
Let the far end rest on the floor so it cannot fall any further
Clamp it tighter in the vice so the overhang is held up
Support the far end on a roller stand at the vice's height
questions.why: A long bar that sags levers the work in the vice and pinches the blade, and a falling end can injure someone. A roller stand at the same height supports it level and lets it slide for each cut.

questions.q: On the 1.5 mm-wall tube, Fabian's 18 TPI blade keeps snagging, and two teeth have broken off. Why?
o: The tube is made of harder steel than the round bar
Too few teeth are touching the thin wall at once
The blade is fitted with its teeth facing forward
He is pressing only on the forward stroke
questions.why: At least three teeth must be in contact. On a 1.5 mm wall an 18 TPI blade has only one or two teeth on the metal, so each catches like a step and snaps; a 32 TPI blade suits thin wall.

questions.q: Fabian's blade breaks halfway through the round bar. After fitting a new blade, how should he carry on?
o: Start a fresh cut from the other side of the bar
Carry on in the old cut, pressing hard to clear it
Turn the new blade back to front for the old cut
Loosen the new blade so it can follow the old cut
questions.why: A new blade is slightly wider than the worn one, so it jams in the old cut and can break or strip its teeth. Starting from another side lets the new blade cut its own kerf to meet the first.

questions.q: Why should Fabian start his cuts on a flat face of the square tube rather than on a corner?
o: A corner makes the kerf too narrow for the blade
Starting on a corner blunts the frame's blade pins
Starting on a flat face needs much less blade tension
On a corner, too few teeth bite and they snag
questions.why: On a sharp corner only one or two teeth touch at a time, so they catch and strip, and the blade skids off the line. A flat face, at a slight angle, gives a steady start with several teeth cutting.

questions.q: A customer asks for some 1.5 mm stainless-steel blanks on the same guillotine. What should Jodi-Ann decide?
o: Cut them, as 1.5 mm is under the 1.6 mm on the plate
Cut them, but press the pedal twice as hard as usual
Not on this guillotine: they are beyond its capacity
Cut them two sheets at a time to share the force
questions.why: The capacity plate is for mild steel. Stainless steel is much stronger in shear, so this machine can cut only about two-thirds as thick in stainless, around 1 mm; 1.5 mm stainless would overload it.

questions.q: How should Jodi-Ann mark the lines that will stay on the finished galvanised trays?
o: Scratch them deeply with a scriber so they last
With a fine marker or pencil, not a scriber
With a centre punch, a dot every 5 mm
With a cold chisel, lightly tapped along
questions.why: A scribed or punched line cuts through the zinc coating, and the bare steel underneath soon rusts, especially in a wet fish market. A fine marker or pencil shows the line without damaging the coating.

questions.q: After a straight cut with snips, the edge of a blank shows a small step about every 30 mm. Why?
o: She opened the snips too wide on each new cut
She used straight snips instead of right-cut snips
She closed the tips fully at the end of each cut
The galvanised coating is too hard for snips
questions.why: Closing the tips fully at the end of each cut leaves a small step or tear. Stop each cut short of the tips and feed the snips forward, keeping long, open cuts.

questions.q: Later in the day, the guillotine starts leaving a heavy burr and bending the edge of the sheet. What should Jodi-Ann do?
o: Press the pedal harder and faster to get a cleaner cut
File every edge afterwards and carry on cutting the blanks
Turn the sheet over so the burr is on the other side
Stop and report it: the blades may be blunt or set wrong
questions.why: A heavy burr and a bent edge on sheet within capacity point to blunt blades or the wrong blade clearance. Setting the blades is a job for a trained person, so she stops, tags it if needed, and reports it.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do with the discs that got soaked and then dried out?
o: Not use them: damp may have weakened the discs
Use them, as they look dry and undamaged now
Use them only at a slower speed than usual
Dry them out further in the sun, then use them
questions.why: Water can weaken the resin bond inside a disc even when it looks fine afterwards, and a weakened disc can burst at speed. Set them aside, report them, and store discs dry in their packaging.

questions.q: What should be done about the painted gate drying in the line of the sparks?
o: Throw a damp cloth over the gate and carry on cutting
Cut quickly so fewer sparks reach the gate
Move the gate, or turn the saw away from it
Carry on, since sparks cool down within 3 m
questions.why: Abrasive sparks travel well beyond 3 m and can ignite wet paint, its fumes or rags. Point the sparks away from anything that can burn, using a screen if needed, before cutting.

questions.q: Kadeem has been pushing the disc down hard. The cut ends are blue and the disc is wearing away fast. What should he change?
o: Push down even harder so each cut takes less time
Let the saw cool, then cut using the side of the disc
Use light, steady pressure and let the disc cut
Cool each cut end with water between every cut
questions.why: Forcing an abrasive disc overheats the work and the disc, wears it out and raises the chance of it breaking. Light, steady pressure cuts cleanly; never use the side of a cutting disc.

questions.q: The tube clamp sticks, so Kadeem starts holding the tube against the vice by hand. What should he do instead?
o: Stop, tag the saw out of use and report the clamp
Wear thicker gloves so his hand is better protected
Hold the tube by hand only for short pieces
Ask a classmate to hold the tube while he cuts
questions.why: Work must be clamped so it cannot move or twist into the disc; held by hand it can grab, kick and break the disc, with hands close to it. A faulty clamp means the saw is out of use until it is fixed.

questions.q: What should be done about the emergency stop that does not work?
o: Keep using the saw and switch it off at its normal switch
Tag the saw out of use and report it at once
Put a note on it so others know to press it harder
Leave it, as the stop is needed only in emergencies
questions.why: An emergency stop that fails leaves no quick way to stop the blade when something goes wrong. The saw must be tagged out and reported, and nobody should use it until it is repaired.

questions.q: What should Oshane do about the coolant spilled on the floor?
o: Leave it to evaporate overnight, as coolant is mostly water
Sweep the chips into it so it soaks up into a paste
Hose the whole area down into the nearest drain
Soak it up, clean the floor and report any leak
questions.why: Coolant on the floor makes people slip, often near a machine with a blade. Clean it up, keep chips and coolant out of drains, and report the leak so it can be fixed.

questions.q: Oshane has switched off and fitted his padlock and tag to the isolator. What should he do before reaching in to clean round the blade guides?
o: Try the start button to prove the saw will not run
Ask a classmate to stand guard by the isolator for him
Take off his safety glasses so he can see clearly
Loosen the blade tension so it cannot move at all
questions.why: Pressing start after locking off proves that the right isolator has been locked and the machine really is dead. Then he returns the switch to off and works with gloves and a brush.

questions.q: Rohan is cutting 45° mitres on 25 mm square tube for a gate panel. What is the best check that a pair of mitres is right?
o: Measure each piece's length to the short point of the mitre
Put the two mitred ends together and check with a square
Compare the two cut faces by eye against the light
Weld the corner and then check whether the frame fits
questions.why: Two correct 45° mitres make a true 90° corner, which a square checks at once. Checking after welding is too late to correct a wrong cut.

questions.q: Monique is cutting copper water pipe with a wheel tube cutter, tightening the knob a full turn at a time, and the pipe is squashing out of round. What should she change?
o: Turn the cutter faster round the pipe each time
Hold the pipe in the vice by its very end
Use the reamer before starting the cut instead
Tighten the knob only a little after each turn
questions.why: A tube cutter works by rolling a thin wheel deeper a little at a time; forcing it squashes thin pipe. Tighten about a quarter turn after each full turn round the pipe, and ream the inside burr afterwards.
